questions.stem: Choose the correct word: The new policy will _____ millions of citizens.
questions.explanation: AFFECT (v) = to influence. EFFECT (n) = a result / outcome; (v, rare) = to bring about. Memory hook: A-ction = Affect verb; Result = Effect noun.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: Honesty is his guiding _____.
questions.explanation: PRINCIPLE (n) = a rule / fundamental truth. PRINCIPAL (n, adj) = head (of school) / chief. Hook: 'The principal is your pal' (adj = main); 'principle' ends in -le like 'rule'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: She bought pens, paper and envelopes from the _____ shop.
questions.explanation: STATIONARY (adj) = not moving. STATIONERY (n) = writing materials. Hook: envelopes = stationEry (both have E). Very high-hit in SSC CGL spelling.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: Her knowledge of physics _____ her engineering skills.
questions.explanation: COMPLEMENT (v/n) = completes, adds to the whole. COMPLIMENT (v/n) = flattering remark. Hook: complEment → complEte.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: An _____ danger forced the evacuation of the area.
questions.explanation: IMMINENT = about to happen (danger, storm). EMINENT = famous, distinguished (person). IMMANENT = inherent, dwelling within (philosophy / theology). Three-way trap loved by setters.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: Teachers must be _____ while grading; a single biased act can harm a career.
questions.explanation: DISINTERESTED = impartial, unbiased (the grading context needs impartiality). UNINTERESTED = bored, not caring. Hook: dis = apart from personal interest.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: The whistleblower refused to _____ the sensitive documents.
questions.explanation: DIVULGE = to reveal secret information. ELICIT = to draw out (a response). ILLICIT (adj) = illegal. ELUDE = to escape. High-hit confusable triangle: elicit / illicit / divulge regularly tested together.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: After drought, the farmers had to _____ to the city in search of work.
questions.explanation: MIGRATE = move from one place to another (general). EMIGRATE = leave one's country (E = Exit). IMMIGRATE = enter a country (I = In). Drought-driven rural-to-urban is internal → migrate.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: He decided to _____ his right to legal counsel.
questions.explanation: WAIVE = to give up a right. WAVE = hand gesture / water motion. 'Waive his right' is the fixed legal register. Also see: 'a waiver' (n, document that waives).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: The minister was _____ for inciting hate speech.
questions.explanation: PROSECUTE = to bring a legal action against (court context). PERSECUTE = to oppress, harass, often on religious/ethnic grounds. High PYQ-hit confusable pair.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The research scholar spent the entire night _____ over ancient manuscripts in the library.

options.option_text: pouring, referring to liquid flowing out rapidly
peering, meaning to look closely at something
poring, meaning to study or read with great care
pondering, meaning to think deeply about facts

questions.explanation: 'Pore over' means to study or examine attentively; it is not related to liquid at all. 'Pour over' describes flowing liquid and is the most common misspelling here. 'Peering' and 'pondering' do not collocate with 'over manuscripts' in the idiomatic sense required.

questions.stem: The new welfare scheme covers all government employees _____ those on contractual appointment.

options.option_text: accept — to receive or agree to something
except — to exclude from a general rule
expect — to consider probable or imminent
exempt — to grant an official exclusion

questions.explanation: 'Except' functions here as a preposition meaning 'excluding'. 'Accept' means to receive or agree to — it cannot introduce an excluded group. 'Exempt' requires a separate grammatical object ('exempt them from'), so it does not fit the blank directly.

questions.stem: By repeatedly ignoring court orders, the accused seemed to _____ the authority of the judiciary.

options.option_text: flaunt — to show off wealth or talent publicly
flair — a natural talent or stylish quality
float — to propose an idea for consideration
flout — to openly defy rules or authority

questions.explanation: 'Flout' means to openly disregard or defy laws and authority. 'Flaunt' means to display ostentatiously — a very common substitution error. The context is deliberate defiance, not display. 'Flair' and 'float' are phonetically similar distractors but contextually absurd.

questions.stem: The court issued an order to _____ the circulation of the book, citing national security concerns.

options.option_text: prescribe — to officially order or recommend
proscribe — to officially forbid or prohibit
describe — to explain or portray in detail
subscribe — to formally agree or register

questions.explanation: 'Proscribe' means to ban or forbid; 'prescribe' means to mandate or recommend (as in medical prescriptions). The distinction is classic PYQ material: a court proscribes banned material, never prescribes it. 'Describe' and 'subscribe' are phonetic traps with entirely different meanings.

questions.stem: The senior officer was asked to _____ the junior of all developments before the press briefing.

options.option_text: apprise — to inform or notify in detail
appraise — to assess the value or quality
appease — to pacify or satisfy a demand
appoint — to assign to a role officially

questions.explanation: 'Apprise someone of something' means to inform or update them. 'Appraise' means to evaluate worth (as in a performance review). The preposition 'of' following the blank is the definitive contextual cue — one apprises someone of something, never appraises them of it.

questions.stem: Though the scientist was _____ to the peer-review process initially, the panel's decision to mandate it proved sound.

options.option_text: adverse — harmful or unfavorable in effect
averted — turned away or diverted from harm
advert — to refer briefly or make mention

questions.explanation: 'Averse to' describes personal reluctance or dislike (a psychological state). 'Adverse' describes external conditions that are harmful (adverse weather, adverse effects). The collocation test is decisive: one is 'averse to' something, never 'adverse to' it. 'Averted' and 'advert' are phonetic traps with entirely different meanings.

questions.stem: From the economist's guarded response about growth figures, the journalist could only _____ that the data was unfavourable.

options.option_text: imply — to hint at something indirectly as the speaker
infer — to draw a conclusion from evidence or hints
implore — to beg or entreat someone urgently
inflect — to modulate pitch or tone of voice

questions.explanation: The journalist (the listener or reader) infers — deduces a conclusion from indirect signals. The economist (the speaker) implies — indirectly suggests something without stating it. Swapping the two is the most frequently tested usage error in this pair. 'Implore' and 'inflect' are phonetically similar but semantically irrelevant distractors.
